For a hypothetical incoming review, suppose the accepted maximum is 0.10 mg KOH/g and a certificate reports 0.08 mg KOH/g using the agreed method. The reported number is below that stated ceiling. This illustrates a comparison against one limit; it does not approve the lot as a whole or establish Chemstock's DOS specification.

Read viscosity with its temperature and reporting instruction

A viscosity entry should identify the unit and temperature alongside the result. If the agreed requirement calls for kinematic viscosity at 40°C, a number reported at another temperature is not automatically evidence against that same requirement. Request the relevant result or have the technical reviewer resolve the difference.

Where the specification says “Report,” record the result as information required by that specification. If the plant also maintains an internal acceptance range, confirm how that range is incorporated into the purchase requirement. Otherwise, the supplier and buyer may be working to different expectations.

Keep historical results available without turning them into an unapproved specification. Previous lots can help the quality team investigate a change, but the highest and lowest numbers seen so far do not automatically define the permitted future range. An approved criterion should state how acceptance is determined.

Handle missing or ambiguous entries before release

If a certificate omits a required parameter, identify the missing field and request the appropriate information. Do not mark the lot acceptable because the other rows look familiar. Likewise, do not infer failure merely because a report uses a different layout; first establish whether the required evidence is present elsewhere in the documentation.

A result described only as “conforms” may require clarification depending on the agreed reporting requirement. Ask whether the purchase calls for a measured numerical result, a conformance statement or another specific format. The requirement should come from the accepted specification and quality process.

When a result is near an acceptance boundary, follow the applicable method and decision rule. Avoid adding an informal tolerance or rounding the figure to create a preferred outcome. Escalate the interpretation to the responsible quality reviewer and retain the resolution with the material record.

Keep a discrepancy review focused on the actual issue

A useful supplier query identifies the material, lot, specification revision, parameter and exact point requiring clarification. That is more actionable than requesting a new certificate without saying why. It also reduces the risk that a revised document changes presentation while leaving the substantive question unanswered.

If the clarification changes the acceptance decision, record who approved it and which requirement applies going forward. The purchasing team should not have to reconstruct the same conversation on the next DOS order. A clear record turns one resolved discrepancy into a more precise future inquiry.

For a new purchase, provide Chemstock with the approved DOS specification and identify any mandatory certificate fields before the material is ordered. That aligns the requested documentation with the plant's acceptance process. The goal is a shipment that can be reviewed against an agreed requirement, with each reported value serving a defined purpose.

Keep incoming inspection separate from application performance

A conforming incoming certificate answers a material acceptance question. It does not replace testing of a complete formulation where the project requires it. For a low-temperature application, define the compound or finished-part test separately instead of treating a DOS viscosity result as proof of flexibility.

The DOS product page identifies the chemical for the inquiry. The DOS low-temperature data guide addresses the separate question of interpreting compound test results. Use the certificate to verify the purchase and application evidence to qualify the use.

title: Sebacic Acid Specifications: Look Beyond the Assay
description: Compare sebacic acid specifications beyond headline purity. A worked ash-limit example shows why matching assay does not establish equivalent purchase limits.
bodyHtml:
Two sebacic acid documents can show the same minimum purity while permitting different limits for another property. A quotation described only as “99.5%” therefore leaves part of the buying decision unresolved. Compare the limits your process requires before treating the offers as equivalent.

Send Chemstock your sebacic acid specification with the inquiry. Identify the required physical form as well as the chemical limits so the proposed material can be reviewed against one complete requirement.

Matching purity can hide another difference

For an illustrative comparison, imagine two specifications with the same 99.5% minimum assay but maximum ash limits of 0.03% and 0.02%. These are hypothetical purchase requirements, not Chemstock offers or claims about available grades. Their matching assay would not make the complete specifications identical.

The useful conclusion is narrow: the headline purity alone does not describe all the limits. It does not follow that every buyer needs the tighter ash limit or that one product is universally better.

Translate the percentage before discussing its importance

At a one-metric-tonne quantity, 0.03% corresponds to 0.3 kg, while 0.02% corresponds to 0.2 kg. This calculation expresses the respective ceilings on that mass basis. It does not mean either shipment actually contains that quantity of ash, and it does not predict a performance difference.

That distinction helps purchasing discuss the issue precisely with the technical owner: does the process require the tighter ceiling, or does the existing acceptance specification permit both? The answer determines which offers belong in the commercial comparison.

Compare limits with limits and results with results

Do not put a supplier's maximum next to another supplier's actual lot result and rank them as if they were equivalent evidence. A maximum states the permitted boundary; a result describes the tested lot.

A useful comparison separates the two:

Document entryPurchasing interpretation
Agreed maximum or minimumThe boundary used for acceptance
Actual lot resultEvidence to evaluate against that boundary
Typical valueReference information unless incorporated into an agreed requirement
Missing propertyA point to resolve where your process requires it

Check the document's grade, form and revision as well. A publicly available sheet is useful research, but the supplier must identify the specification applicable to the offered material.

Identify the basis of each percentage

An assay number is meaningful only with its stated measurement and reporting basis. When two sebacic acid documents use the same percentage, ask the technical reviewer to confirm that the entries are comparable. The same numerical minimum does not, by itself, establish that the analytical methods or reporting conventions are identical.

Keep the original parameter description alongside the value in the comparison sheet. If one document leaves the basis unclear, request clarification instead of silently assigning the basis used by the other. This is particularly important when an internal purchasing system reduces a complete specification to a few short fields.

The purpose is not to make every inquiry more complicated. It is to resolve differences that affect acceptance before purchasing ranks the offers. Once the requirement is established, future quotes can refer to the accepted specification rather than repeating the same open questions.

Separate moisture limits from actual received content

A moisture maximum establishes a boundary in the applicable specification. It does not describe the actual moisture of every shipment. If a hypothetical limit is 0.30%, its arithmetic equivalent is 3 kg per 1,000 kg of material on that stated mass basis. That is a ceiling calculation, not a measurement of a delivered lot.

Do not deduct the full maximum from every invoice quantity as though it were known actual content. If the commercial comparison requires a correction for measured content, the technical and commercial teams must establish the appropriate basis and use the relevant results. A specification limit alone is insufficient for that adjustment.

The same distinction applies when discussing assay. A minimum is not an exact lot result, and a tighter minimum is not an automatic prediction of process performance. Use the accepted requirements to identify eligible material, then compare actual offers for that requirement.

Compare ash limits without inventing a process benefit

In the earlier hypothetical example, the difference between maximum ash limits of 0.03% and 0.02% is 0.01 percentage point. On a 1,000 kg basis, that corresponds to a difference of 0.1 kg between the ceilings. It does not establish the difference between two actual lots.

Ask the process owner whether that limit matters to the intended use and which criterion is required. If the accepted specification permits both limits, the tighter one may not justify an additional cost for that application. If the process requires the tighter ceiling, an offer that does not meet it belongs outside the like-for-like price comparison.

Avoid describing ash as a specific contaminant unless the relevant analysis supports that identity. A general ash result is not a complete identification of individual components. If the application needs limits on particular substances, those requirements should be stated explicitly and reviewed with the appropriate technical evidence.

Do not treat separate analytical rows as a simple recipe balance

Assay, moisture and ash entries have distinct definitions and methods. Do not assume that subtracting two listed maxima from 100 produces the expected assay, or that the rows can be added to reconstruct every component in the material. Have the technical owner establish any relationship needed for a particular evaluation.

For purchasing, the practical approach is to compare each required row against its own acceptance criterion. Keep method references and document revisions available. That avoids creating a misleading combined score from numbers that were not intended to function as a single mass-balance calculation.

If a supplier provides an additional property, decide whether it answers an actual application need. More rows do not automatically make an offer better. A complete purchasing specification contains the criteria necessary for the accepted use, with a clear basis for evaluating them.

Use a requirement matrix before reviewing the price

Create a short matrix with the plant's requirement in the first column and each offered grade in the next columns. For every required property, record the offered limit and whether any clarification remains open. Add physical form as a separate requirement so that a chemically acceptable powder is not mistaken for an approved granular material.

Use plain statuses such as meets the stated requirement, does not meet it, or needs clarification. A missing value belongs in the third category until it is resolved. It should not receive a favorable assumption simply because the headline purity is familiar or the price is attractive.

Once the technical owner identifies the eligible offers, compare their actual package quantities, delivery charges and commercial terms. This sequence makes the price comparison more useful because each option represents a material the plant can accept under the same defined requirement.

Review a specification revision as a change record

If a new offer cites a different specification revision, compare the relevant rows with the accepted version. Identify changed limits, methods, physical descriptions and reporting requirements. Ask the technical owner to decide which changes affect approval rather than assuming that a later revision is automatically interchangeable.

Retain the accepted revision with the purchase record. A future buyer should be able to determine which requirement governed the order without searching through a series of emails. When a revised requirement is approved, update the purchasing reference deliberately so that old and new versions do not circulate as equally current instructions.

Turn the approved requirement into an actionable inquiry

Send Chemstock the accepted sebacic acid specification, required physical form and quantity, together with the delivery requirement. If an alternative limit or form can be considered, identify the part that is open to evaluation and the person or process responsible for approval.

That creates a useful distinction between a firm purchasing requirement and a possible sourcing alternative. Chemstock can review the stated need, and your technical team can assess any proposed difference explicitly. The resulting quote comparison is grounded in the material your operation requires, rather than a headline assay that leaves the rest of the specification undecided.

Complete the comparison with the physical form

Chemical limits do not answer whether the plant requires powder or granules, or what a sieve requirement means. Keep that issue explicit rather than burying it under a general description of purity. The sebacic acid sieve-specification guide explains the retained-versus-passing distinction.

Once the required limits and form are established, use the sebacic acid catalogue reference to request the quantity you need. Purchasing can then compare prices for material that meets the same stated requirement.
